record.original_question: A pair of primes is called a twin-prime pair when the two primes differ by 2, so the pair has the form (p, p+2). Are there infinitely many primes p such that both p and p+2 are prime?

evidence.quote: A pair of primes are said to be twin primes if their difference is 2, i.e. the pair is of the form (p, p+2). The twin prime conjecture states that there are infinitely many primes p such that p+2 is also a prime.

artifact.self_contained_problem: A prime number is a positive integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. A pair of primes (p, p+2) is called a twin-prime pair. Prove or disprove: there exist infinitely many primes p such that p+2 is also prime.
artifact.status_search_result: The twin prime conjecture remains a famous open problem in number theory. Significant partial progress has been made: Zhang (2013) proved that there are infinitely many prime pairs differing by at most some finite constant (originally 70,000,000), subsequently reduced by the Polymath8 project and Maynard–Tao to 246, but the full conjecture (gap exactly 2) is still unresolved as of 2026.

status_evidence.title: Twin prime conjecture - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The twin prime conjecture states that there are infinitely many twin primes... still an open problem.
status_evidence.claim: The twin prime conjecture is currently open, with Zhang's and Maynard's bounded-gaps results as the strongest known partial progress.
